chain.g: the art of painting, a painting

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English picture, from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”), from pingō (“to paint”). Doublet of pictura.

senses.d: A representation of anything (as a person, a landscape, a building) upon canvas, paper, or other surface, by drawing, painting, printing, photography, etc.
An image; a representation as in the imagination.
ex: My eyes make pictures when they are shut.

senses.d: A painting.
ex: There was a picture hanging above the fireplace.
Here the stripped panelling was warmly gold and the pictures, mostly of the English school, were mellow and gentle in the afternoon light.

senses.d: A photograph.
ex: I took a picture of the church.
Pictures of Lily made my life so wonderful / Pictures of Lily helped me sleep at night

senses.d: A motion picture.
ex: Casablanca is my all-time favorite picture.
"You make moving pictures. In jungles and places." "That's me. And I've picked you for the lead in my next picture."

senses.d: ("the pictures") Cinema (as a form of entertainment).
ex: Let's go to the pictures.

senses.d: A paragon, a perfect example or specimen (of a category).
ex: She's the very picture of health.

senses.d: An attractive sight.
ex: The garden is a real picture at this time of year.

senses.d: The art of painting; representation by painting.
ex: any well-expressed image[…]either in picture or sculpture

senses.d: A figure; a model.
ex: the young king's picture[…]in virgin wax

senses.d: To represent in or with a picture.
ex: What is striking about the self portrait is that the patient had pictured herself as a much younger woman

senses.d: To imagine or envision.
ex: Picture yourself on a boat on a river / With tangerine trees and marmalade skies
If you can picture this—a day in December / Picture this—freezing cold weather / You got clouds on your lids and you'd be on the skids

senses.d: To depict or describe vividly.
ex: Drawing is picturing people, places, and things with line.
Many rock paintings picture various species of fish.

grp.label: representation of visible reality produced by drawing, etc

ety.text: Inherited from Old French image, borrowed from Latin imaginem (“a copy, likeness, image”).
Inherited from Latin quadrum.
From Latin imāginem (“image, imitation”), from Proto-Italic *imā (“copy”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym- (“copy”). Doublet of imago, and also the now-archaic mania.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin imāginem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese figura, fegura, borrowed from Latin figūra.

pt:imagem.gl: image; picture; figure (optical representation of an object)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese ymagen, omagen, omage, from Latin imāginem (“a copy, likeness, image”), from *im-, also the root of imitor (“to copy, imitate”).
Clipping of photographie.
From foto- + -grafia.
Clipping of fotografia.
Clipping of fotografía.
From foto- + -grafía.

fr:cinéma.gl: cinema, filmmaking (the art of making films and movies)

ety.text: Clipping of cinématographe.
Clipping of cinema, from Ancient Greek κῑ́νημα (kī́nēma, “movement”).

pt:cinema.gl: cinema; movie theater (building where films are shown to an audience)

chain.g: cinema, filmmaking (the art of making films and movies)

ety.text: Borrowed from French cinéma, reduction of cinématographe, ultimately from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “movement”).

From Middle English piken, picken, pikken, from Old English *piccian, *pīcian (attested in pīcung (“a pricking”)), and pīcan, pȳcan (“to pick, prick, pluck”), both from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”). Doublet of pitch and peck. Cognate with Dutch pikken (“to pick”), German picken (“to pick, peck”), Old Norse pikka, pjakka (whence Icelandic pikka (“to pick, prick”), Swedish picka (“to pick, peck”)).

senses.d: A tool used for digging; a pickaxe.
An anchor.
ex: It's better to amble around, drop the "pick" for a lunchtime swim or beachcomb, then find a nice anchorage for the night.

senses.d: A pointed hammer used for dressing millstones.
A tool for unlocking a lock without the original key; a lock pick, picklock.
A comb with long widely spaced teeth, for use with tightly curled hair.
A tool used for strumming the strings of a guitar; a plectrum.
A pike or spike; the sharp point fixed in the center of a buckler.
ex: Take down my buckler […] and grind the pick on 't.

senses.d: A choice; ability to choose.
ex: France and Russia have the pick of our stables.

senses.d: That which would be picked or chosen first; the best.
Pasture; feed, for animals.
ex: ‘She's all African grass and Brahmans. There's not a blade of native pick left, except on the ridges.’

senses.d: To grasp and pull with the fingers or fingernails.
ex: Don't pick at that scab.
He picked his nose.

senses.d: To harvest a fruit or vegetable for consumption by removing it from the plant to which it is attached; to harvest an entire plant by removing it from the ground.
ex: It's time to pick the tomatoes.

senses.d: To pull apart or away, especially with the fingers; to pluck.
ex: She picked flowers in the meadow.
to pick feathers from a fowl

senses.d: To take up; especially, to gather from here and there; to collect; to bring together.
ex: to pick rags

senses.d: To remove something from somewhere with a pointed instrument, with the fingers, or with the teeth.
ex: to pick the teeth; to pick a bone; to pick a goose; to pick a pocket
Did you pick Master Slender's purse?

senses.d: To decide upon, from a set of options; to select.
ex: I'll pick the one with the nicest name.
She had to pick her steps to avoid the flutters of the quivering, bleeding bodies.

senses.d: To seek (a fight or quarrel) where the opportunity arises.
To recognise the type of ball being bowled by a bowler by studying the position of the hand and arm as the ball is released.
ex: He didn't pick the googly, and was bowled.

senses.d: To pluck the individual strings of a musical instrument or to play such an instrument.
ex: He picked a tune on his banjo.

senses.d: To open (a lock) with a wire, lock pick, etc.
ex: The lock was of a kind that Watt could not pick. Watt could pick simple locks, but he could not pick obscure locks.

grp.label: to grasp and pull with fingers
to remove a fruit or plant for consumption
to decide upon, from a set of options; to select

From picco + -one.
Inherited from Old Spanish bico, from Latin beccus, possibly from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos. It was phonetically influenced by the verb picar (“to peck”). Compare English beak.

es:sacho.gl: a kind of hoe or mattock

From zapa + pico.

pt:picareta.gl: pickaxe (heavy tool used to break rocks)

From Grimaldo, Romance form of the Germanic name Grimwald, perhaps once thieves' slang or used jokingly; compare German Dietrich (“picklock”).
Borrowed from Basque gantzua.

Inherited from Middle French choix, from Old French chois, deverbal from choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *keusan (see contemporary Dutch kiezen), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”).
From scegliere.

pt:escolha.gl: choice (opportunity to choose or select something)

ety.text: Deverbal from escolher (“to choose”).

Inherited from Middle French prendre, from Old French prendre, prandre, from Latin prēndere, alternative form of prehendere (“to seize”), from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, seize”) (not attested without prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

Inherited from Old French coillir, formed analogically, with the verbal suffix -ir, from cueil, stressed conjugated form of the original cueudre, cueildre, cueldre, from Latin colligere (“collect”), from con- (“with, together”) + legō (“bring together, gather, collect”). Doublet of colliger.

it:prendere.gl: to take, hold, pick up, get

ety.text: Inherited from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendere (“take, seize”) (not attested without a prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.
From Old Spanish furgar, from Vulgar Latin *fūricāre, from Latin fūr (“thief”) whence English ferret and furtive.

inherited from Late Latin *sculcāre, often derived from a Proto-Germanic *skulkan and connected to English skulk (“to hide”) and Norwegian Nynorsk skulke (“to play truant”), though this is disputed by Rance.

es:escarbar.gl: to paw, scratch, scrape, dig (the ground)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish escarvar, from Latin scarīfāre, from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”). Cognate with English scarify, Galician escarvar.
Inherited from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), from pix (“pitch”).
From Latin recolligere. Compare Sicilian ricògghiri.

ety.text: Inherited from Latin recolligere. Doublet of recolegir, a borrowing. Compare English recollect.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese colher, from Latin colligere (“to collect, to gather”). Compare also the borrowed doublets coligir and coligar. Cognate with Galician coller, Asturian coyer, and Spanish coger.

Inherited from Middle French choisir, from Old French choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *kauʀijan (“to choose”) or Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (kausjan), both from Proto-Germanic *kauzijaną, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose, taste”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose, taste”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exēligere, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēligere.

Inherited from Old Spanish escoger, equivalent to es- + coger, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Asturian escoyer, Catalan escollir, Extremaduran escogel, Galician escoller, Portuguese escolher.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escolher, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician escoller, Spanish escoger, Catalan escollir.
From picture + -esque, a calque of French pittoresque, from picture (“a picture, painting”).

senses.d: Resembling or worthy of a picture or painting; having the qualities of a picture or painting; pleasingly beautiful.
ex: We looked down onto a beautiful, picturesque sunset over the ocean.
A dear old lady said she thought the ancient castle at Conway most picturesque, but that it was a pity they put it so close to the railway!
senses.zh: 繪畫般的；逼真；栩栩如生

senses.d: Strikingly graphic or vivid; having striking and vivid imagery.
ex: picturesque language

senses.d: An informal social gathering, usually in a natural outdoor setting, to which the participants bring their own food and drink.
ex: We went out for a picnic in the forest.

senses.d: The meal eaten at such a gathering.
An easy or pleasant task.
ex: We remind the guests that dealing with this problem is no picnic, and to be patient.

senses.d: An entertainment at which each person contributed some dish to a common table.
A cut of pork from the shoulder area (above the front leg) of a pig.
ex: Smoked picnics (calas) are pork shoulders with the butt portion removed just beyond the knuckle bone. Shoulder butts are boneless […]

senses.d: To take part in a picnic.
ex: And I'll never forget the chillingly instinctive racism. "Sure is pretty countryside. Pity it's spoiled by the niggers picknickin."

senses.d: In a record player, an electromagnetic component that converts the needle vibrations into an electrical signal.
Electromagnetic coil receiver of metal string oscillations.
The reception of sound, etc. by such a device.
ex: This microphone has very weak pickup.

senses.d: Impromptu or ad hoc, especially of sports games and teams made up of randomly selected players.
ex: Rather than join a basketball league, James decided to play pickup.
At lunch we had a game of pickup hockey.

senses.d: An instance of approaching someone and engaging in romantic flirtation and courting with the intent to pursue romance, a date, or a sexual encounter.
ex: Hey, thanks for the drink, but if this is a pickup, I'm not interested.
"Sunday Music," a chronicle of a disco pickup and morning after that skillfully parallels Eric's recollections of a recent ex-lover.

senses.d: A person successfully approached in this manner for romance or sex.
ex: "Good Lord! I'm not stopping you from taking on all the pick-ups that come your way."
Audball's latest pickup didn't seem to care where they were, or anything at all about alimony, palimony, or child support […]

senses.d: In various games, the fielding or hitting of a ball just after it strikes the ground.
An item that can be picked up by the player, conferring some benefit or effect; a power-up.
ex: Every step of the way you come across absolutely loads of aliens, pick-ups and new and weird obstacles to overcome.

senses.d: The act of a challenging party or candidate winning an electoral district held by an incumbent party or candidate.
ex: The returns from the election show Apple Party candidate Jane Doe has made a pickup in the district of City West defeating Orange Party Incumbent Joe Smith

senses.d: The act of answering a telephone.
ex: That's why the phone at the theater's on automatic pickup.

grp.label: act of collecting and taking away, usually in a vehicle

ety.text: From Middle English dragge, from Old Norse draga (“that which is dragged, dragged load”), from Proto-Germanic *dragǭ (“sledge, sled”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to haul, pull”). Cognate with English dray.
